## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

The first year of the Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program for the Dokie 1 Wind Energy Project (the Project) was completed in 2011. The purpose of the Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program is to verify the accuracy of the effects on birds and bats predicted in the Environmental Assessment (EA) and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures undertaken by Dokie Wind Energy Inc. (DWEI). The 2011 surveys included bird and bat mortality monitoring, transect surveys for migrating songbirds on stopover, and breeding bird surveys. This report summarizes the data collected for the Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program in 2011 and compares the results to data collected for the Project in 2007 (baseline), 2008 (during construction), and 2009 (after vegetation clearing).

Project construction activities began on the site in March 2008. Five turbines were installed in 2008 and remained idle until 2011. There were no construction activities in 2009. Project construction was completed in 2010 and commercial operations started on February 16, 2011. Activities on site in 2011 included: reclamation, turbine maintenance, environmental monitoring, and wildlife monitoring.

The purpose of the mortality monitoring program is to record bird and bat mortality associated with the operational phase of the Project, to verify the accuracy of the effects predicted in the EA, and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures put forward in the EA Application. The mortality monitoring program was divided into three periods to capture high collision-risk periods for birds and bats: spring migration (March 17 to May 30), breeding season for songbirds (June 1 to 20), and fall migration (August 4 to October 19). Mortality monitoring searches were conducted according to Environment Canada (2007) protocols: searches were once every three days, within a 50 m radius of the turbine base, at 24 of the 48 turbines.

Mortality estimates for birds and bats are affected by: searcher efficiency (individual differences in searcher ability to detect carcasses), scavenger impact (the proportion of carcasses _not_ removed by scavengers), and proportion of area searched (the proportion of area searched within a 50 m search radius at each turbine). Correction factors for each of these sources of bias were incorporated into mortality estimates following the guidelines outlined by the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (2010a, 2010b) and Environment Canada (2007).

A total of 25 carcasses were found during the mortality monitoring period in 2011. Twenty-two carcasses (including 16 birds and 6 bats) were found during formal mortality monitoring surveys: 9 during the spring migration period, 2 during the breeding season, and 11 during fall migration. The majority of carcasses were of songbirds. No raptors were found during mortality searches during the entire survey period. Six bat carcasses were found during mortality searches: 2 during spring migration (May 9 and 10) and 4 during fall migration (August 5, September 1 and 2). This includes five silver-haired bats and one little brown myotis. None of the species found during the mortality monitoring period were federal or provincial species at risk.

The estimated bird mortality rate for the Project is 3.38 birds per turbine (1.13 birds per MW) from March 17 to October 19, 2011; equivalent to 162 birds extrapolated across all 48 turbines over the monitoring period. For bats, the estimated mortality rate is 1.27 bats per turbine (0.42 bats per MW)

from March 17 to October 19, 2011; equivalent to 61 bats across all 48 turbines over the monitoring period. Mortality rates for birds was not related to weather (i.e., wind speed, temperature, and humidity); while for bats, all mortalities were found following nights with average wind speeds below 6.5 m/s. These results indicate that mortality at the Dokie 1 Wind Energy Project is low relative to reported ranges across North America (National Wind Coordinating Committee 2010).

Transect surveys were conducted to monitor use of the Project area as a stopover site by songbirds in 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2011 in spring and fall migration. The purpose of the surveys is to verify the predictions from the EA that the effects of the Project on stopover site usage by songbirds would be low. To test the Project effects, transect surveys were conducted at both control transects (in forested habitats further away) and impact transect (adjacent to operating turbines). Transects were surveyed before construction (2007), during construction (2008), after vegetation clearing (2009), and during operations (2011). Overall, habitat use of Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge by birds on stopover was lower in 2011 compared to previous years. Both bird abundance and species richness was lower overall, and in several migratory periods the effect was more pronounced on impact transects than on control transects.

Breeding bird surveys were conducted to monitor the effect of Project construction and operation on the abundance and distribution of songbirds breeding in the Project area. Stations were established and surveyed in 2007 (before construction) and surveyed again in 2008 (during construction), 2009 (after vegetation clearing), and 2011 (operations). Point count surveys were conducted at stations on Johnson Col and Jonson Ridge and results were compared to surveys at stations on the nearby Spruce Ridge which served as a control site. The results of the breeding bird surveys do not indicate an effect of the Project on habitat use by songbirds during the breeding season; the patterns of bird abundance and species richness were similar at both Johnson Col (impact) and Spruce Ridge (control) across the four years of study. However, at Johnson Ridge, bird abundance and species richness were slightly lower after vegetation clearing for the project (2009 and 2011) compared to surveys during construction in 2008.

The potential effects of the Project on habitat use by birds in 2011 include: loss of habitat from the Project, loss of habitat from forestry (on Johnson Col), disturbance from construction activities, and disturbance from operating turbines. This habitat loss and disturbance has reduced habitat usage by migrating and breeding birds near turbines on the Project site. The results of the habitat use surveys (transect surveys and breeding bird surveys) are consistent with the prediction in the EA that there would be an adverse effect of the Project on habitat use by birds but that the effect on the population would be low.

Stantec recommends that the 2012 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program continue to monitor potential effects of the Project on birds and bats. The program should include: mortality monitoring surveys for birds and bats from mid-March to mid-October, migration stopover surveys in May and August, and breeding bird surveys. The results in 2012 will be compared to data collected in previous years and used to verify the accuracy of the predicted effects on birds and bats in the EA, and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures.

## **1 INTRODUCTION**

## **1.1 Background and Project Overview**

Dokie Wind Energy Inc. (DWEI) has constructed Phase 1 of the Dokie Wind Energy Project (the Project) in the Peace River Regional District, approximately 40 km west of Chetwynd, BC. The Project includes 48 3-MW wind turbines on two ridge tops (Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge) and associated infrastructure including access roads, collector lines, and the substation.

Project construction activities began on the site in March 2008. Construction activities included: 1) tree and vegetation clearing for turbine foundations, assembly areas, roads, transmission lines, substations and gravel pit; 2) road building; 3) construction of the substation and turbine foundations; 4) erection of power line poles; and, 5) erection and commissioning of turbines. Five turbines were installed in 2008 and remained idle until 2011. There were no construction activities in 2009. Project construction was completed in 2010 including: installation of the remaining 43 wind turbines, installation of the collector lines and transmission line, completion of the substation, and minor road construction and maintenance.

Commercial operations started on February 16, 2011. Activities on site in 2011 included: reclamation, turbine maintenance, environmental monitoring, and wildlife monitoring.

The Project area is within two biogeoclimatic zones: Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir and Boreal White and Black Spruce. The Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir zone occurs at high elevations and is forested habitat dominated by Englemann spruce and subalpine fir. Occasionally Lodgepole pine and black spruce are present at lower elevation sites. Portions of the Project area are within the Boreal White and Black Spruce BEC zone. These forests are dominated by subalpine fir and hybrid white spruce. Black spruce is found in upland areas alongside lodgepole pine, within wetland habitats. These forested areas provide habitat for songbirds, raptors, and bats during breeding and migration.

The ridges are also part of a migration corridor for raptors and nocturnally migrating songbirds. The Environmental Assessment (EA) considered the potential effects (and associated mitigation measures) of mortality, habitat alteration, and sensory disturbance on migratory birds (including raptors) and bats. Based on studies completed in support of the EA, effects of the Project on birds and bats were predicted to be low. However, due to uncertainty in the underlying mechanisms of bird and bat mortality at wind farms, a follow-up program was recommended.

## **1.2 Regulatory Context**

As part of the Project’s Environmental Assessment Certificate (E06-03), issued under the _BC Environmental Assessment Act_ , DWEI committed to implement operational wildlife monitoring. Natural Resources Canada (NRCan), as a Responsible Authority for the Project under the _Canadian Environmental Assessment Act_ (CEAA), also determined that a follow-up program is appropriate for the Project.

CEAA defines ‘follow-up program’ as a program to:

- Verify the accuracy of the environmental assessment, and/or

- Determine the effectiveness of any measures taken to mitigate adverse environmental effects.

The 2011 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program was executed according to the Wildlife Monitoring Plan (Version 7.0, December 8, 2010). The Wildlife Monitoring Plan was designed to verify the predictions of the EA and was prepared to meet the provincial and federal requirements for the Project related to potential effects on birds and bats.

## **1.3 Purpose**

The purpose of the Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program is to verify the accuracy of the effects on birds and bats predicted in the EA and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures undertaken by DWEI. The timing and frequency of surveys for the Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program were designed to capture the peak activity periods as follows (Table 1–1):

- **Mortality Monitoring** —At representative turbines during spring and fall migration and breeding seasons to monitor direct mortality of birds and bats.

- **Migrant Stopover Surveys** —Transect surveys for migrants in spring (May) and fall (August) to compare to data collected at the same transect locations surveyed in pre-construction at control and impact sites on Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge.

- **Breeding Bird Surveys** —Point-count surveys in June to compare to data collected at the same stations surveyed during pre-construction on impact (Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge) and control sites (Spruce Ridge) to test project effects.

## **2 BIRD AND BAT MORTALITY MONITORING**

## **2.1 Introduction**

Wind energy projects are known to cause mortality of birds and bats. Bird mortality is generally a result of direct collisions with wind turbines whereas bat fatalities are caused by barotrauma (Barclay _et al_ . 2008). Barotrauma is tissue damage that occurs due to a rapid air pressure reduction near the moving turbine blades. Studies on the abundance and distribution of birds, conducted as part of the EA process, predicted that the risk of mortality for birds and bats at the Project would be low. The key mitigation measures to reduce mortality risk from wind turbines are:

- **Project Location** —The project is not located near important bird colonies significant staging or wintering areas for waterfowl or shorebirds, significant areas of bird concentrations, or near an area recognized as nationally important for birds (e.g., National Wildlife Area, Migratory Bird Sanctuary, Important Bird Area, National Park, Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network).

- **Turbine Siting** —Individual turbines are located away from the edges of ridges.

The purpose of the mortality monitoring program is to record bird and bat mortality associated with the operational phase of the Project, to verify the accuracy of the effects predictions in the EA, and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures.

The mortality monitoring program was divided into three periods to capture high collision-risk periods for birds and bats:

- **Spring Migration** —March 17 to May 30 for northward migrating raptors, song birds, and bats

- **Breeding Season** —June 1 to June 20 for song birds and bats

- **Fall Migration** —August 4 to October 19 for southward migrating raptors, song birds, and bats.

## **2.2 Field Methods**

Mortality monitoring searches for birds and bats were conducted according to methods outlined in the Wildlife Monitoring Plan (Version 7.0; December 8, 2010) and with protocols recommended by Environment Canada (2007) and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (2010a, 2010b). Searches were conducted by two individuals: a Stantec biologist and a First Nations Field Searcher. Searches were conducted once every three days at 24 of the 48 turbines (Figure 1–1). The same 24 turbines were searched throughout the monitoring program. In general, every other turbine was searched; however priority turbines in high risk areas (e.g., the ends of each ridge, high and low points along either ridge) were also targeted.

Mortality monitoring was also conducted at a one kilometre segment of collector line on the north end of Johnson Ridge that was identified as a high collision-risk area for birds. The collector line was surveyed approximately once per week during spring migration and breeding bird season. The collector line surveys did not continue during fall migration because bird diverters were installed on the line in late July. In addition to regular carcass searches, DWEI staff and contractors were instructed to identify and report any injured or dead birds and bats located on site to document mortalities detected outside of formal survey periods.

In accordance with Environment Canada protocols (2007) searches for bird and bat mortalities were confined to a 50 m radius around each turbine. Each surveyor searched one half of each turbine pad by walking transects spaced 5 m apart (Photo 2–1). Carcass searches were suspended during hazardous weather conditions (e.g., heavy snow, ice buildup on turbines, thunder and lightning, etc.) or when maintenance activities prevented safe access to a turbine (Photo 2–2); however, the searching schedule was adjusted when needed to maintain equal sampling effort at each turbine.

The date each turbine was searched and the weather conditions for each search are summarized in Appendix A.

If a dead bird or bat was located, observers recorded:

- Date and time of observation

- Location (distance and direction to nearest turbine and geographic coordinates)

- Species, where possible

- State of decomposition and estimated number of days since death

- Descriptive features (e.g., colour, size) of carcass remains.

Carcasses or remains (i.e., feathers) were photographed and collected (if necessary) for species identification. Carcasses found in reasonable condition were used for searcher efficiency or scavenger impact trials (see Section 2.3). These activities were conducted in accordance with permits from Environment Canada (BC-SA-0070-11) and the BC Ministry of Environment (FJ10-66111). The permits are included in Appendix B.

## **2.3 Data Analysis and Correction Factors**

Mortality estimates for birds and bats are affected by the following factors:

- **Searcher Efficiency** —Individual differences in searcher ability to detect carcasses.

- **Scavenger Impact** —The proportion of carcasses _not_ removed by scavengers.

- **Proportion of Area Searched** —The proportion of area searched within a 50 m search radius at each turbine.

Correction factors for each of these sources of bias were incorporated into mortality estimates. Because each of these could be influenced by seasonal factors (e.g., snow cover conditions, turbine pad reclamation), the correction factors were applied specifically for each season. The correction factors used followed the guidelines outlined by the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (2010a, 2010b) and Environment Canada (2007).

## **Searcher Efficiency**

Individual searchers vary in their ability to find carcasses. Searcher efficiency trials are designed to account for those differences and provide data to correct mortality estimates for that source of bias.

For searcher efficiency trials the “tester” placed a “test” bird or bat carcass within the 50 m search boundary of a turbine pad prior to carcass searches that day. The “tester” recorded the location (UTM), species, and the ground cover (i.e., gravel, soil, snow, etc.) where the carcass was placed. If the trial carcass was not found, the “tester” retrieved it at the end of the day to determine if it was scavenged or if it was missed by the searcher. The trials were conducted as randomized blind tests for each searcher. For each trial, the bird species to be used (including an option for multiple birds or ‘no bird’) and the turbine location for the trial, was selected randomly.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted two to three times each week throughout the sampling period to account for seasonal differences in searcher efficiency based on ground cover (i.e., snow versus bare ground). Trials were repeated 2 to 12 times per searcher. The “test” carcasses were obtained from the BC Ministry of Environment (via University of Northern British Columbia). Test carcasses included songbird, raptor, and grouse species likely to occur within the region. Two bats, found during carcass searches, were also incorporated into searcher efficiency trials.

Searcher efficiency (Se) was calculated for each searcher according to Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (2010a, 2010b) as the proportion of non-scavenged carcasses found by individual searchers:

_**Se = (# test carcasses found) / (# test carcasses placed – # test carcasses scavenged)**_

Survey effort and searcher ability varied throughout the monitoring period. To account for this, overall searcher efficiency was calculated by weighting efficiency rates of searchers according to the proportion of turbine surveys completed by each individual over each season, as:

## _**Se = Se1 (n1/T) + Se2 (n2/T) + ... + Sx (nx/T)**_

where:

_**Se**_ is the overall searcher efficiency for each season

_**Se1** to_ _**Sex**_ are the individual searcher efficiency ratings

_**n1** to_ _**nx**_ is the number of turbines surveyed by each searcher

- _**T**_ is the total number of turbines surveyed by all searchers.

## **Scavenger Impact**

Scavengers (such as crows, ravens, and carnivorous mammals) are known to remove bird and bat carcasses at wind energy projects. To account for this, scavenger trials were conducted according to Environment Canada (2007) protocol. Trials involve distributing carcasses in known locations at turbines throughout the Project area and revisiting them approximately every two days over a two week period to determine the rate of removal. Scavenger trials were conducted on an on-going basis. However, to prevent scavenger swamping (which can occur if the capacity of scavengers to remove or consume carcasses is exceeded), there were no more than five active trials at any time (Smallwood _et al._ 2010). Nineteen species of bird and one bat species were included in trials to account for differences in scavenger rates by carcass size, colour, or scavenger type. Species used in scavenger trials are listed in Appendix C.

The proportion of carcasses remaining after each two day search interval was used to calculate the overall scavenger impact correction factor ( _**Sc**_ ):

_**Sc = (n visit 1 + n visit 2 + n visit 3+...+ n visit 6) / (n visit 0 + n visit 1 + n visit 2+...+ n visit 5)**_

where:

_**Sc**_ is the proportion of carcasses not removed by scavengers over the search period _**n visit 0**_ is the total number of carcasses placed

_**n visit 1** to_ _**n visit 6**_ are the number of carcasses remaining on each visit 1 through visit 6.

The scavenger impact correction factor was calculated for each season for songbirds and bats.

## **Proportion of Area Searched**

Post-construction monitoring data from Ontario suggests that most birds and bats fall within 50 m of a wind turbine base and recommend that the maximum search area be within that 50 m radius (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources 2010a, Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources 2010b). However, it is not always possible to search the entire 50 m radius due to dense vegetation, or steep or inaccessible terrain. Mortality monitoring searches were limited in area to the extent of the turbine pad (which was generally less than 50 m in radius). Mortality estimates were corrected for the proportion of the area not searched.

The proportion of area searched within a 50 m search radius of the turbine was measured by observers using the tracking function on a handheld Geographic Positioning System (GPS) unit and walking the perimeter of the search area at each turbine. The perimeter track was later uploaded and the search area was calculated using Geographic Information Systems (GIS).

The proportion of area searched was determined seasonally for each turbine ( _**Psx**_ ) as:

_**Psx = (area searched within 50 m radius) / π (50)[2]**_

The average proportion of area searched (Ps) was then calculated for all surveyed turbines:

_**Ps = Ps1 + Ps2 + ... + Ps24 / 24**_

## **Mortality Estimates**

The following calculation was used (as recommended in Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, 2010a) to estimate the overall bird and bat mortality rate per turbine:

## _**C = c / (Se x Sc x Ps)**_

where:

_**C**_ is the corrected number of bird or bat fatalities _**c**_ is the number of carcasses found

_**Se**_ is the proportion of carcasses expected to be found by searchers (searcher efficiency) _**Sc**_ is the proportion of carcasses not removed by scavengers over the search period (scavenger impact)

_**Ps**_ is the proportion of area searched.

This mortality estimate per turbine was then extrapolated to estimate overall mortality for all of the 48 turbines of the Project over the monitoring period.

## **2.4 Results**

## **Searcher Efficiency**

A total of 88 searcher efficiency trials were conducted between March 17 and October 19. Trials were conducted for the five observers that participated in searches during spring migration, the four observers during the breeding season, and the six observers during fall migration (Table 2-1). Individual searcher efficiency (Se) ranged from 0.50 to 0.80 during the spring migration period, 0.50 to 0.77 during the breeding season, and 0.50 to 1 during fall migration. To account for variation in survey effort between searchers, overall searcher efficiency was calculated by weighting efficiency rates of searchers according to the proportion of the total surveys they completed over the season.

## **2.5 Discussion**

## **2.5.1 Bird Mortality**

The National Wind Coordinating Collaborative (2010) reports that bird mortality rates at wind facilities across North America range from 0 to 14 birds per MW per year; the bird mortality rate at the Dokie 1 Wind Energy Project (1.13 birds per MW) is at the low range of that estimate. The bird species found were of common birds that are abundant at the Project site. Kinglets (ruby-crowned and golden-crowned kinglets) and dark-eyed juncos were the most common species found during mortality surveys (Table 2–3). During spring migration, songbird carcass mortality was concentrated over two weeks (from May 1 to May 14). During fall migration, carcasses were found over ten weeks (from August 5 to October 18). Songbird mortality was not related to broad patterns in wind speed, temperature, or humidity.

There was no raptor mortality recorded at the Project site in 2011. Raptors observed during migration monitoring in 2011 were recorded flying at greater heights, above the rotor swept area of turbines, than in previous years (N. Johnston, pers. comm.). This avoidance behaviour reduces mortality risk and likely contributed to the lack of raptor mortality.

## **2.5.2 Bat Mortality**

The estimated bat mortality rate recorded at the Dokie 1 Wind Energy Project (0.42 bats per MW) is low compared to bat mortality rates recorded at other facilities across North America, which ranges from 0 to 39 bats per MW per year (NWCC 2010). The National Wind Coordinating Collaborative has identified that bat mortalities at wind facilities across North America coincide with peak migration periods for bats. Silver-haired bats are thought to migrate seasonally from the northern United States and southern British Columbia to summer breeding sites in northern British Columbia; whereas little brown myotis are residents of northeastern British Columbia year-round (Nargorsen and Brigsen 1993). In British Columbia, silver-haired bat migration peaks in spring (May and June) and early fall (August and September; Nargorsen and Brigsen 1993). Bat mortalities were concentrated in midMay and early September and likely coincide with the timing of migration. The National Wind Coordinating Collaborative (2010) suggests that tree-roosting bat species are most at risk of collision. Tree-roosting species may be attracted to turbines when seeking suitable foraging habitats such as those provided by the open areas of cleared turbine pads (Strickland _et al_ . 2011). One little brown myotis (a resident bat species) carcass was found in early August. This individual was likely using habitat in the Project area for foraging and roosting, increasing the risk for contact with turbines.

Bat activity is known to be higher on clear, calm nights; increasing the potential for turbine-related mortality (Baerwald and Barclay 2011, Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources 2010b, NWCC 2010). Weather records indicated that bat carcasses were often found at the Project following evenings of low wind speed compared to monthly averages (Table 2-6). The 2012 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program will continue to monitor bat mortality. Stantec recommends that the program include surveys to investigate the potential for mortality of early migrating bats during July.

## **2.5.3 Carcass Distribution**

Nineteen of the 25 carcasses (76%) found during the mortality monitoring period for the Project were on Johnson Ridge which includes 68% of the turbines. The number of carcasses detected at a single turbine ranged from zero to three. Turbines that are located near the ends of ridges or along depressions in ridge top topography were assumed to be areas of greatest concern (Baerwald and Barclay 2011); however, the carcasses detected were evenly spread throughout the site. Stantec recommends that the 2012 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program continue to investigate potential patterns in the distribution of carcasses throughout the Project site.

## **3.1 Migrant Passerines on Stopover**

## **3.1.1 Introduction**

Transect surveys were conducted to monitor use of the Project area as a stopover site by songbirds in 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2011 in spring (northward) and fall migration (southward). Studies on the abundance and distribution of birds conducted as part of the EA process predicted that the effect of habitat alteration and sensory disturbance from the Project on migratory birds would be low. The purpose of the surveys is to verify the predictions from the EA.

To verify the predictions and test the effects of the Project, habitat use by migrating songbirds will be compared among years at both control and impact transect locations. Impact transects were located in areas close to construction activities and operating turbines while control treatments were positioned in areas further from operating wind turbines and where vegetation clearing did not occur (Figure 3-1). Transects were surveyed before construction (2007), during construction (2008), after vegetation clearing (2009), and during operations (2011).

## **3.1.2 Field Methods**

Transect surveys for migrating songbirds were conducted according to methods outlined in the Wildlife Monitoring Plan (Version 7.0; December 8, 2010) and with protocols recommended by Environment Canada (2007). Ten transects (Figure 3-1), each 500 m long, are located on Johnson Ridge (four) and Johnson Col (six). Transect locations were selected based on habitat type, access, and proximity to construction activities associated with the Project. On Johnson Col there are four impact transects and two control transects and on Johnson Ridge there are two impact and two control transects. Table 3-1 provides a description of the change in habitats from before construction (baseline) to Project operation.

Survey methods were similar among years. Observers walked each transect over a 30 minute period, recording the species, abundance, behaviour, distance along transect, distance from observer, and height for each bird observed within 100 m of either side of the transect. Surveys generally began at sunrise and continued for four hours. In order to eliminate bias associated with the start time and location, the transect order was changed daily. Weather parameters (temperature, wind speed and direction, cloud cover, precipitation) were recorded at the start and end of each transect; however, surveys were suspended during periods of heavy precipitation or high winds (< 3 on the Beaufort Wind Scale). In 2011, each transect was surveyed four times during the spring (May 3 to 10) and fall migration period (August 17 to 25) to account for daily changes in the abundance and richness of birds observed in the Project area.

## **3.1.3 Data Analysis**

Mixed general linear models (GLMs) were used to test for an effect of the Project on the abundance and species richness of migrating birds. The data were analysed to test for differences in relative bird abundance (number of individuals detected per observation hour) and species richness (number of species per observation hour) between years and between control and impact transects (treatment). Transect was included in the model as a random factor to account for repeated sampling of the same transect. All 2-way interactions were included in the model and non-significant terms (P > 0.05) were removed sequentially until the minimum adequate model was derived. Means and their 95% confidence intervals (C.I.) are reported throughout.

## **3.1.4 Results**

## **3.1.4.1 Relative Abundance**

At Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge, data for each migratory period was analyzed separately because the effects of the Project were different between spring and fall migration periods. The number of individuals of each species detected on transect surveys is provided in Appendix D.

At Johnson Col, during spring migration, the number of birds (mean ± 95% C.I.) recorded was different among years and between control and impact transects (Figure 3-2). In 2011, during

operations, there were fewer birds observed on both control and impact transects (6 ± 13) compared to previous years (2007: 24 ± 11; 2008: 29 ± 10; 2009: 24 ± 12). Furthermore, in 2011 there were disproportionately fewer birds observed on the impact transects (1.9 ± 14) compared to controls (11 ± 22). Though the effect was only marginally statistically significant (GLM: year X treatment; F3, 75=2.1, P=0.10, N=85), this result indicates an effect of Project operations on habitat use by migrating birds.

During fall migration bird abundance was different among years but did not differ between control and impact transects (Figure 3-2). There were significantly fewer birds observed (GLM: effect of year; F3, 81=11.0, P < 0.001, N=90) in both 2008 during construction (25 ± 9) and 2011 during operations (9 ± 11); compared to both 2007 before construction (44 ± 11) and 2009 after vegetation clearing (42 ± 8). Though bird abundance differed among years; it was similar between control and impact transects (GLM: year X treatment; F3, 81=0.6, P=0.62).

## **3.1.5 Discussion**

During migration, habitat use of Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge by birds on stopover was lower in 2011 compared to previous years. Both bird abundance and species richness was lower overall; in several migratory periods the effect was more pronounced on impact transects (adjacent to operating turbines) than on control transects (in forested habitats further away). These results are consistent with the prediction in the EA that there would be an adverse effect on habitat use by migrating songbirds but that the effect on the population would be low.

During spring (northward) migration bird abundance was lower in 2011 than in previous years. Furthermore, it was disproportionately lower on impact transects compared to control transects. This

result suggests that project activities may have had an adverse effect on abundance of birds using these habitats on migration. During fall (southward) migration, bird abundance was lower during construction (2008) and operations (2011) compared to before construction (2007) and after vegetation clearing when the site was idle (2009).

Species richness was also lower in 2011 than in previous years. This is consistent between spring and fall migratory periods and at both control and impact transects. Several species were relatively common previously but were not observed in 2011. These include: Lincoln’s sparrow, white-throated sparrow, orange-crowned warbler, Wilson’s warbler, and pine grosbeak (see Appendix D).

Vegetation removal was completed for roads and turbine pads for the Project in 2008 however, in 2010, West Fraser Mills also cleared a large amount of bird habitat on Johnson Col for forestry purposes. Therefore in 2011, total potential effects on migrating birds included: habitat loss from the Project, additional habitat loss from forestry, noise from operating turbines, and disturbance from construction activities on-site. Bird abundance was disproportionately lower on impact transects compared to control transects during spring migration. In spring, there were more construction activities compared to fall, which may explain why abundance was disproportionately lower on impact transects during spring migration. Noise from operating turbines not only may reduce bird usage of adjacent habitats, but also affects an observer’s ability to hear birds. At Johnson Col control transects are located in open areas without a forested buffer to dampen the noise from the turbines.

On Johnson Ridge during spring migration, bird abundance declined from 2008 to 2009 and again in 2011 on both control and impact transects. During fall migration bird abundance was similar at control transects among years but declined in 2011 at impact transects. These results are also consistent with an effect of Project activities on bird abundance during migration.

On Johnson Ridge, fewer species were observed during spring migration in 2009 and 2011 than in 2008 at both control and impact transects. During fall migration, species richness was similar between years at control transects; however at impact transects, the number of species declined from 2008 to 2009 and again in 2011. There were nine species observed on surveys during spring migration in 2008 (during construction) that were not recorded in 2009 (after vegetation clearing when the site was idle) or in 2011 (operations). During fall migration there were 13 species recorded in 2008 but not in 2009 or 2011. Many of these species were forest birds (e.g., hairy woodpecker, northern flicker, and Townsend’s warbler [see Appendix D]).

In 2011, potential effects on migrating birds on Johnson Ridge included: habitat loss from the Project, noise from operating turbines, and disturbance from construction activities on-site. Unlike Johnson Col, at Johnson Ridge the control transects are in forested habitats where the sound from operating turbines is dampened. On these transects observers can effectively detect and identify birds by song or call.

## **3.2.2 Field Methods**

Point count surveys for breeding birds were conducted between 0430 (sunrise) and 0930 hours. At each station, the time, location (GPS), and weather parameters (temperature, wind speed and direction, cloud cover, precipitation) were recorded, however surveys were suspended during periods of heavy precipitation or high winds (< 3 on the Beaufort Wind Scale). A ten minute survey was conducted by two observers at each station where each bird was identified by song or sight within 75 m of the station. Observers estimated the distance (m) and direction (degrees) of each bird relative to the observer, and recorded the species, sex, behaviour, and time of each observation. Point count surveys were conducted twice during the breeding season from 2007 to 2009 (early and late June) and once in 2011 (mid-June).

## **3.2.3 Data Analysis**

Mixed general linear models (GLMs) were used to analyze breeding bird abundance and species richness. Station was included as a random effect to account for repeated sampling of the same station. Weather variables, time, date, and ridge were included to test for effects of the Project on bird abundance (number of individuals detected per station) and species richness (number of

species detected per station). All 2-way interactions were included in the model and non-significant terms (P > 0.05) were removed sequentially until the minimum adequate model was derived. Means and their 95% confidence intervals (C.I.) are reported throughout.

## **3.2.5 Discussion**

The results of the breeding bird surveys do not indicate an adverse effect of the Project on habitat use by songbirds during the breeding season. The patterns of bird abundance and species richness were similar at both Johnson Col (Impact) and Spruce Ridge (Control) across the four years of study. Both bird abundance and species richness were slightly lower in 2008 (construction) and 2009 (aftervegetation clearing) compared to 2007 (baseline) and 2011 (operations); however, there were no statistically significant differences between years. The most common species at all three ridges have remained consistent among survey years.

At Johnson Ridge, bird abundance and species richness were slightly higher in 2008 (during construction) than in 2009 (after vegetation clearing) and in 2011 (operations). During the 2008 breeding bird surveys, vegetation clearing and grubbing at Johnson Ridge was largely complete, however site grading had not occurred and the wood waste piles had not been removed. This provided some habitat for shrub and ground nesting birds compared to 2009 and 2011 when that habitat was removed. The width of habitat removal along Johnson Ridge is over 100 m, which exceeds the radius of a point count circle. There is less remaining forested habitat within point count circles compared to Johnson Col; which may in part explain why bird abundance and species richness is lower on Johnson Ridge post-construction.

## **4 SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS**

The monitoring data collected during the 2011 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program are consistent with predictions of the EA that there would be adverse effects of the Project on birds and bats but that the effects would be low.

A total of 25 carcasses were found during the mortality monitoring period in 2011. Bird mortality is estimated to be 3.38 birds per turbine (1.13 birds per MW), extrapolated to 162 birds over the 48 turbines; and bat mortality is estimated to be 1.27 bats per turbine (0.42 bats per MW), equivalent to 61 bats over the 48 turbines during the monitoring period. These results indicate that mortality at the Dokie 1 Wind Energy Project is low relative to reported ranges across North America (National Wind Coordinating Committee 2010). Overall, the low mortality rates are consistent with the predictions of the EA and suggest that the mitigation measures implemented for the Project (i.e., Project location and turbine siting) were effective.

Results of the transect surveys for migrants on stopover indicate that, in general, bird use of the site by songbirds was lower in 2011 than in previous years. During migration, habitat use of Johnson Col and Johnson Ridge by birds on stopover was lower in 2011 compared to previous years. Both bird abundance and species richness was lower overall; in several migratory periods the effect was more pronounced on impact transects (adjacent to operating turbines) than on control transects (in forested habitats further away).

The results of the breeding bird surveys do not indicate an effect of the Project on habitat use by songbirds during the breeding season; the patterns of bird abundance and species richness were similar at both Johnson Col (Impact) and Spruce Ridge (Control) across the four years of study. However, at Johnson Ridge, bird abundance and species richness were slightly lower after vegetation clearing for the project (2009 and 2011) compared to surveys during construction in 2008.

The potential effects of the Project on habitat use by migrants and breeding birds in 2011 include: loss of habitat from the Project, loss of habitat from forestry (on Johnson Col), disturbance from construction activities, and disturbance from operating turbines. This habitat loss and disturbance has reduced habitat usage by migrating and breeding birds near turbines on the Project site. The results of the habitat use surveys are consistent with the prediction in the EA that there would be an adverse effect of the Project on habitat use by birds but that the effect on the population would be low.

Stantec recommends that the 2012 Operational Wildlife Monitoring Program continue to monitor potential effects of the Project on birds and bats. The program should include: mortality monitoring surveys for birds and bats from mid-March to mid-October, migration stopover surveys in May and August, and breeding bird surveys. The results in 2012 will be compared to data collected in previous years and used to verify the accuracy of the predicted effects on birds and bats in the EA, and to determine the effectiveness of mitigation measures.
